top_choice_rationale: P002 (Pakes, Berry and Levinsohn, B012) is my first choice on achievement, maturity and attribution. The random-coefficients demand framework (Berry 1994; Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes 1995) recovers substitution patterns, markups and welfare from market data. It has stayed the working standard through about three decades of identification and computational critique, and it changed merger review, antitrust and applied work in several fields. The three-name set is the compact joint core, and a narrow citation on demand estimation for differentiated products and industry competition avoids implying credit for all of empirical IO. The omissions (Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard, Levin) are a real cost, and I would reverse my order if the record showed Bresnahan's contribution to be equal in kind to BLP. P001 (Kiyotaki and Moore, B002) is a close second. It has the cleanest two-author credit and an original mechanism that is distinct from the 2022 prize. The size of collateral amplification is still weakly identified, though, and I weigh that against it. Its broad support is not evidence of merit and does not enter my ranking. P000 is last because both substantive proposals describe mature, bounded achievements that I judge worth recognising.
recusal_note: No personal connection to Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn, Kiyotaki or Moore appears in my profile. Disclosures: I am an affiliated professor at the Stockholm School of Economics, as are committee members Dreber Almenberg, Friberg and Strömberg. Strömberg also supports P002, so I do not treat that agreement as independent confirmation. My own field of matching, auctions and market design is adjacent to the B012 area and may incline me toward it, and I discount that. I do not adjudicate these disclosures.
